data.title: Trump meets Putin for first time in 15 months, talks Ukraine
data.description:
US PRESIDENT Donald Trump and Russian leader Vladimir Putin discussed Ukraine during their first in-person meeting in more than a year on Thursday (Nov 19) on the sidelines of a gathering of world leaders in China.

“We’ve had a great relationship for many years, we know each other for a long time and I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start,” Trump said after shaking hands with Putin.

The roughly 40-minute encounter unfolded in Shenzhen, where both were attending the annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit.

On entering a small meeting room on the sidelines of Apec, Trump said, “Who is he? He’s my friend.”

Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent were also present as part of the US delegation, and also had handshakes with the Russian leader.

Putin left the meeting in “excellent spirits”, Russia’s state-run Tass news service said, citing Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov. The talks went well and focused primarily on the war in Ukraine, Ushakov said.

At the start of a separate bilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, Trump said that he was looking to both Putin and Xi for help “with respect to the war with Russia and Ukraine. I’d like to see it ended”.

The trio are set for a historic trilateral meeting later in the day. Trump said he felt “very strongly, I think something will come” from that sit-down.

The direct talks between Trump and Putin – away from Ukrainian representatives – are likely to intensify fears in Europe about the two leaders making major decisions on the war that could force stark concessions on Ukraine. 

Trump has ramped up US efforts to broker a ceasefire, as Russia’s war on its neighbour nears its five-year mark.

Putin continues to make demands for Ukrainian territory he does not control and is hammering its cities with drone and missile strikes.

Trump, though, has insisted the Russian leader is eager to end the war and has been casting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as the bigger obstacle to peace.

Trump and Putin shook hands during gatherings with other Apec leaders on both Wednesday and Thursday, in their first personal interactions since an August 2025 summit in Alaska.

That meeting on American soil had offered Putin a prominent international stage, undercutting efforts to isolate Russia over its war – but failed to provide the diplomatic breakthroughs Trump sought.

The US president had vowed to end the war on his first day back in office, though has since conceded it is a far more daunting task. 

European concerns

Trump’s Asia trip, which included a stop in the Philippines, also marks the US president’s first travel overseas since his Republican Party lost control of Congress in midterm elections, giving him an opportunity to bolster his own standing overseas.

Whether he will seek to do that at the expense of Ukraine has many foreign capitals on edge.

European allies want credible security arrangements to ensure Russia does not violate any truce, and they have been unnerved by comments from Trump envoy Jared Kushner that the US was ready to discuss a “broader European security architecture” – remarks seen as bending to Kremlin demands and weakening Nato.

Kyiv’s allies have long insisted Russia first stop the fighting before discussions about Nato or troop movements.

There has been little indication Putin is ready to do so.

Ukraine has sought to demonstrate its own military strength and ramp up the costs on Russia for its invasion.

On Tuesday, Ukraine struck a key bridge between mainland Russia and occupied Crimea, and later followed up with attacks on two oil refineries in Russia’s southern region.

Even as Trump has pushed diplomatic talks on the war he has sought an opening to bolster longer-term business and commercial opportunities between the US and Russia.

Ahead of the US midterms – in which high costs of living including for energy were the dominant issue for voters – he announced a deal with Putin for Russia to supply diesel to the global market.

That move drew bipartisan blowback, with critics saying that it would only help Russia fund its war. Efforts to find buyers for the Russian diesel have also stalled. Analysts are sceptical any of those supplies will end up being delivered to the US. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Stocks to watch: Jardine Matheson, Riverstone, Deluge
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Wednesday (Nov 18):

Jardine Matheson: The Hong Kong-based conglomerate expects to post a 2026 dividend of at least US$2.50 per share, amid “strong performance” for the third quarter ended Sep 30. This comes after Jardine Matheson raised its full-year profit guidance in October to between US$5.50 and US$5.65 per share on an underlying basis, from the previous guidance of US$5.33 per share. For Q3, its Indonesian unit Astra International’s underlying net profit rose 11 per cent. Shares of Jardine Matheson closed 1 per cent or US$0.62 lower at US$59.15 on Tuesday, before the news.

Riverstone : The glove maker posted a 34.7 per cent rise in net profit to RM70.1 million (US$17.1 million) for the third quarter ended September. Riverstone’s Q3 revenue rose 27.3 per cent to RM315.1 million, marking the group’s highest quarterly revenue in over three years. It also announced that CEO Wong Teek Son will step down on Dec 1, to be succeeded by Chong Chu Mee. Riverstone shares closed 2.1 per cent or S$0.015 higher at S$0.745 on Tuesday, before the results.

Deluge : The fire detection and protection company has secured S$18.5 million in new contracts across Singapore and Malaysia, bringing its cumulative contract wins since January 2026 to more than S$147.7 million. The latest awards span infrastructure, marine and offshore, residential and industrial projects, including a Penang data centre project. Shares of Deluge closed 0.8 per cent or S$0.005 lower at S$0.605 on Tuesday.

data.title: Arm CEO Haas approached by Nvidia boardâs recruitment firm to replace Jensen Huang
data.description:
ARM CHIEF executive officer Rene Haas has been approached regarding the CEO role at Nvidia by recruiting firm Heidrick & Struggles, which was hired by the board to recommend a replacement for Jensen Huang, according to a person familiar with the process. 

Heidrick & Struggles has begun the process of reaching out to executives who might be able to take on the job after Huang left the company last week, according to the person, who asked not to be identified because the process is not public.

Nvidia and Arm representatives did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Nvidia, the world’s largest chipmaker, cut ties with Huang on Nov 12, after revelations about his extramarital affairs spurred a widening scandal.

Huang has admitted to a relationship with a woman that the US government has investigated for spying on behalf of China. Beijing has denied the espionage plot.

Hiring Haas would bring in someone with a history at Nvidia. He served for seven years at the company as general manager of computing products.

Nvidia also attempted to acquire Arm in 2020, though the merger eventually broke down in the face of regulatory opposition.

But the 64-year-old Haas – or anyone else stepping into the Nvidia CEO role – would come under intense pressure. It is arguably the highest-profile job in the tech industry, and the new leader will need to confront a corporate culture shaped around the personality of one man: Huang.

Haas spoke about Huang’s departure during a tech conference in Austin on Wednesday (Nov 18), describing his old boss as “a legend”.

“What he built at Nvidia is historic,” Haas said. “You don’t have many champions like that.” BLOOMBERG

data.title: US-based Cequence Security opens Singapore office as it eyes Asia-Pacific growth
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Privately held US cybersecurity firm Cequence Security is positioning Singapore as its Asia-Pacific headquarters as it expands its presence in the region.

The Santa Clara, California-based company opened its Singapore office on Nov 1.

Cequence Security founder and CEO Ameya Talwalkar told The Business Times that the company plans to hire an initial leadership team of three to five people over the next 18 months. 

The Singapore office will grow in line with business performance and its team will also oversee other teams in the region, Talwalkar said.

The initial hires are expected to focus on sales, with technical roles to be added later, he said.

Cequence already “works with several entities” in Singapore, said Talwalkar. He declined to name them, but said they include both public- and private-sector organisations in telecommunications, financial services, retail and commercial aviation.

Asia-Pacific accounts for about a third of Cequence’s revenue. Its notable clients in the region include Japan’s NTT Docomo and Philippine Airlines.

The company has not disclosed its full financial results. Talwalkar said it expects to break even next year, based on its current business trajectory.

Founded in 2014, Cequence initially focused on bot defence, including measures to stop automated attacks and the creation of fake accounts. It later expanded into application programming interface (API) security as attacks increasingly included the APIs behind apps as well.

The company is now positioning itself as a provider of security solutions for artificial intelligence agents.

Talwalkar said that the use of AI agents by enterprises and individuals will only increase in the coming years as companies seek greater efficiency and individuals look for convenience. 

For example, Cequence’s solutions can help companies to assess if a transaction is being made by an AI agent or a human. The solutions can be tailored to a specific company’s comfort level with allowing the external use of agents. 

“Some customers are welcoming of agents. What they don’t want is agents having revenue impacting interactions, so like a telco has told us never let them cancel a plan, change their passwords or downgrade their plans,” he said. 

Talwalkar also cited a Fortune 50 bank in the US that works with Cequence. The bank does not want external AI agents to make bookings for customers using its exclusive dining services. Instead, it wants customers to use its own enterprise AI agents for such reservations. Cequence’s solutions can help the bank distinguish between external agents and those operating within its own systems, the CEO added.

Talwalkar expects such discussions and decisions to become more common in Singapore and across the Asia-Pacific, which he said has generally been receptive to AI adoption.

“Singapore is a fast follower of agentic AI after the US, that’s our analysis,” he said. “There’s a lot of innovation happening all the way from government agencies to the private sector.”

He also sees the Philippines, Vietnam and Indonesia making rapid progress in adopting agentic AI.

Talwalkar acknowledged that larger competitors offer similar solutions, but said their products tend to focus either on internal cybersecurity or on threats originating outside an organisation. He said that Cequence is the only company that straddles both.

“We were able to solve this problem for some very large telcos in the US. We understood all the challenges they had in securing their infrastructure and then interacting with their customers as well,” he noted.

data.title: Same AI price, very different costs: what to automate in South-east Asia
data.description:
A CUSTOMER opens a chat to dispute a charge. Resolving it takes a staff member about 20 minutes.

In Singapore, that costs the company about US$7.90. In Indonesia, it costs about US$0.60.

Yet, a leading customer service software firm charges the same price in both markets for an artificial intelligence agent to handle that chat.

Board members across South-east Asia are now asking their executive teams which workflows to hand to AI agents.

Our answer is that the business case depends on where the work is done. We compare the cost of the staff who do the work today with the cost of the AI that would do it instead.

The cost of a workflow

We cover six markets: Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines and Indonesia. Our staff costs are based on official wage data for clerical or similar roles, and a 50 per cent addition for employer contributions, supervision and tools.

One customer service software firm charges from US$0.99 each time its AI agent resolves a chat. But AI agents may not be fully autonomous in customer service, so our calculations factor in human staff costs.

The same software firm reports that its AI agent resolves three chats in four on average. Results vary widely by business, so we assume a more cautious scenario, where the AI resolves six chats in 10. Staff still handle the other four.

The human part of the job then moves from routine handling to reviewing and deciding. The staff checks one in 10 chats, taking three minutes each time.

For a business handling 20,000 chats a month, we assume half a full-time employee is required just to manage and maintain the agent.

By our calculations, at US$0.99 per outcome and even after a business pays for the staff it still needs, an AI agent cuts the cost of a chat in Singapore by about half.

In Malaysia, it cuts the cost by about a quarter, and in Thailand by about a tenth. In Vietnam, it saves nothing. In the Philippines and Indonesia, it adds to the cost.

These figures are illustrative estimates based on a single workflow and average wages, which mask wide variances between firms. In reality too, large clients often negotiate published prices down.

Our calculation also excludes the cost of building an agent, connecting it to existing systems and keeping it up to date as models change.

Businesses must therefore run the math using their own data.

The success rate matters too. If the agent resolves only half of all chats, the savings in Singapore fall to about 40 per cent.

If the agent resolves three in four, the savings rise to about 60 per cent. Singapore still saves the most and Indonesia still loses the most.

The reference firm charges for each chat its agent resolves. In higher-wage markets where staff cost more than about US$1 a chat, an agent with a higher resolution rate saves more money.

But where staff costs less, as in the Philippines and Indonesia, every extra chat the agent resolves actually adds to the cost.

The “build vs buy” variable

Some firms build their own agents rather than buy one from a vendor. For them, the choice of AI model matters a great deal.

For this scenario, we estimated costs for six leading models, based on their published prices. (Models we studied were Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 3.8 Flash, GLM-5.2, DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen 3.5.)

With the cheapest model, the self-built AI agent costs less than staff in every market. With the most expensive, it costs more everywhere except Singapore.

Engineering also makes a difference. When building an agent, design can directly affect the bottom line.

Take a mid-priced model: An agent that wastefully rereads twice as much company material at every step would lose its savings in Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines and Indonesia.

An agent engineered to cache material, instead of rereading it, would pay off in all six markets.

Does running AI locally shift the case?

Today, most AI models run in a few giant data centres, mostly outside South-east Asia, and are sold at one global price.

As more countries insist on data sovereignty, keeping data and AI processing at home, more AI is likely to run locally. It would then carry local costs, including power and the cost of meeting each country’s rules and regulations.

Power is the easiest of these costs to measure. Electricity for a data centre costs about three times as much in Singapore as in Indonesia. Still, that makes the same AI only about 10 per cent more expensive.

By contrast, staff costs nearly 13 times as much. So even if AI runs locally, wages are likely to decide where AI agents make commercial sense. The cost of compliance is the open question.

Moving prices and looking beyond costs

Leading AI companies currently spend far more than they earn.

OpenAI expects to burn through about US$280 billion between 2026 and 2030, according to company projections reported by the Financial Times.

Prices may therefore rise. On our estimates, if a mid-priced model trebled its token prices, the savings from AI would disappear everywhere in South-east Asia except Singapore.

Exchange rates add a second risk. AI prices are set in US dollars. A weaker ringgit, baht, dong or rupiah makes the AI agent more expensive in local terms, while local salaries stay roughly the same.

Still, costs may not be the only consideration. AI agents work around the clock; they can absorb sudden peaks in demand, help launch new services faster and create new ways to serve customers.

Where an AI agent saves little in operating costs, these benefits could still justify deploying one.

What leaders should do

Start with the process. Map each workflow and remove unnecessary steps. Every step an AI agent performs adds cost.

Then ask three simple questions of each workflow: One, what does it cost us today? Two, what will it cost with an AI agent, including the staff it still needs? Three, how far could AI prices rise, or the local currency fall, before the business case fails?

Answer these questions separately for each market. Where the savings are small or negative, name the other benefits you expect in advance and measure them.

Crucially, businesses should keep the decision reversible for as long as possible.

Once teams are reshaped around AI agents, the know-how to do the work without them may be lost, and rebuilding that is slow and costly.

A phased roll-out is sensible. Each phase shows what the agent can handle before more of the workflow depends on it.

Avoid tying the workflow to a single provider or model. If that provider changes its terms, retires a model or fails, the business should be able to switch without starting over.

AI may cost the same in every market, but the case for it is won or lost, workflow by workflow and market by market.

Daniel Liebau is an adjunct associate professor with the Asian Institute of Digital Finance at the National University of Singapore, and the founding managing director of Lightbulb Capital, an innovation advisory firm. Damien Kopp is the founder and managing director of RebootUp, an AI advisory firm, and associate faculty, executive development, at Singapore Management University.

Workings are available from the authors on request.

data.title: Motoring tycoon Peter Kwee is back in court: Here are his previous legal battles
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Motoring tycoon Peter Kwee is under the media spotlight again, after losing an appeal on Wednesday (Nov 18) to reclaim five properties in his daughter Karen Kwee’s name.

He had argued that Karen held the properties in trust on his behalf and he was the rightful beneficial owner. The court found that while the evidence supported this, the trust was set up with fraudulent intent to hide assets from creditors.

“We find that as the trust was set up by Mr Kwee for the purpose of concealing the properties from his creditors, it is void and unenforceable as being illegal and contrary to public policy,” the Court of Appeal said.

The properties and rental proceeds from them therefore belonged to Karen Kwee, the court added.

The appeal judgment follows a 2025 trial in which Peter Kwee lost his lawsuit against Karen Kwee’s bankruptcy trustee Lai Seng Kwoon.

With the appeal dismissed, Kwee was ordered to pay Lai S$80,000 in costs.

Peter Kwee’s journey

Kwee was born in 1947 in Bandung, Indonesia, to a couple from China’s Fujian province. At 18, he started a trading business in flour and plastics.

He and his wife Catherine, with their two children, Kevin and Karen Kwee, arrived in Singapore in 1978.

Kwee made a name for himself in Singapore after he became a distributor of Renault and Volkswagen vehicles through his company, Group Exklusiv, in the early 2000s. Senior motor industry figures described Kwee as “a good operator”, “unassuming and clever”, “low key” with “some surprise up his sleeve”.

The veteran businessman soon expanded into property, acquiring a major stake in a resort and then Meadow Springs Golf and Country Club, both in Perth.

At home, Kwee bought Laguna National Golf and Country Club from NatSteel for S$131 million in 2001. A year later, he bought The Pines Club for more than S$100 million.

Clubs and courts

Here are some of the high-profile court cases involving Kwee over the years.

1. Indonesian coal mining billionaire Low Tuck Kwong - Low and his company sued Kwee and another individual for A$9.6 million (US$6.4 million) over alleged material defects, after buying out their shares in a group of companies that own properties.

- These companies’ assets include a hotel, two country clubs with a golf course each, and residential properties in Australia, based on the statement of claim on Nov 13, 2025.

- Singapore-born Low was the fourth-wealthiest person in Indonesia in 2025, Forbes reported.

2. Laguna club

Kwee’s Laguna National Golf and Country Club is world-renowned. It features two notable 18-hole golf courses and has hosted tournaments from the European Tour, Asian Tour and Korean LPGA Tour. Former World No 1 Tiger Woods has also graced its fairways.

Incorporated in 1991, the club was taken over in 2001 by Laguna Golf Resort Holding, a unit of Kwee’s Group Exklusiv.

The first batch of club members each bought a S$120,000 unsecured note to fund the development of the club. These notes were due to mature in June 2021. The members also paid membership fees ranging from S$40,000 to S$180,000.

A day before the unsecured notes were to be redeemed, Kwee notified the club’s trustees that the club was unable to fulfil the redemption due to its financial situation.

In February 2023, the High Court granted an application by pioneer club member Lim How Teck to wind up the club. Around 580 holders of unsecured notes, including Lim, were owed an estimated S$187.4 million stemming from the default over the bonds.

Last year, Kwee, his son Kevin Kwee and their firm were sued for S$71.5 million in damages by the club and its liquidators for allegedly wrongfully and fraudulently extracting and transferring value out of the club to enrich themselves.

3. The Pines Club The Pines Club closed its Stevens Road premises for renovations in 2013, with management promising new facilities. However, Exklusiv Resorts subsequently sold the land to developer Oxley, who built two hotels there.

In October 2017, members were informed that the club had failed to secure a new lease at Stevens Road. They were offered access to facilities at Laguna National Golf and Country Club and Dusit Thani Laguna Singapore, affecting about 1,300 members.

Some 170 members sued Kwee and Exklusiv Resorts, seeking more than S$110,000 each for alleged deceit, negligence and breach of contract. The court upheld only the breach-of-contract claim, awarding each member nominal damages of S$1,500.

Claims on properties

The five properties in question were bought between 1995 and 2000, and registered in Karen Kwee’s sole name.

These are West Georgia and Lord Stanley in Vancover, Canada, King’s Drive and Teneriffe in Singapore, and Spyglass Grove in Australia.

The three-storey semi-detached house at King’s Drive in Bukit Timah was the subject of another lawsuit involving businessman Low Kai Yang.

Low, who called himself Karen Kwee’s “former friend”, claimed that the property was used to secure an S$800,000 loan he agreed to lend to her, an arrangement Karen disputed.  

Low sued in 2022 and the older Kwee intervened, claiming beneficial ownership of the property. The claim was subsequently discontinued.

data.title: Lenovo posts 48% revenue jump on AI-related sales, beating estimates
data.description:
[BEIJING] China’s Lenovo reported a 48 per cent jump in second-quarter revenue, beating analyst estimates, on strong growth in artificial intelligence-related sales such as servers and other hardware.

Revenue rose to US$30.2 billion, above an LSEG consenus estimate of US$27.6 billion drawn from six analysts.

Under Hong Kong accounting standards, the company posted a net loss of US$640 million, compared with a net profit of US$340 million a year earlier.

But Lenovo also said that it booked, under different accounting standards, adjusted net profit of US$1.4 billion, up 166 per cent.

The adjusted figure strips out non-cash accounting items linked to warrants and convertible bonds that Lenovo issued as part of its strategic partnership with Alat, a manufacturing and technology company in Saudi Arabia.

The Infrastructure Solutions Group, which makes servers and data centre equipment, had its strongest quarter ever, with revenue climbing 178 per cent year on year to US$11.3 billion.

AI-related revenue rose 79 per cent to US$10.8 billion, comprising 36 per cent of the group’s total revenue.

Lenovo’s personal computer, tablet and smartphone division, which accounted for about 60 per cent of total revenue during the quarter, grew 15 per cent. REUTERS

data.title: Stocks to watch: Yangzijiang Shipbuilding, Seatrium, Frencken
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Thursday (Nov 19):

Yangzijiang Shipbuilding : The shipbuilder’s subsidiary has entered into an investment agreement with China’s Taicang Port Economic and Technological Development Zone. The agreement is in relation to a project to develop a clean energy vessel intelligent manufacturing base in Taicang city, located in Jaingsu province. The group expects capital expenditure for the project to be about 3.38 billion yuan (US$507 million). Shares of Yangzijiang Shipbuilding ended 1.6 per cent or S$0.07 higher at S$4.39 on Wednesday, before the announcement.

Seatrium : The offshore, marine and energy specialist reported that its net order book stood at S$12.2 billion as at end-September, comprising 35 projects with deliveries extending through 2033. It had secured S$1.7 billion in new orders so far this year. Seatrium expects its underlying net profit for FY2026 to be materially higher than in FY2025. The counter ended 0.6 per cent or S$0.01 lower at S$1.71, before the news.

Frencken : The technology manufacturer announced on Wednesday (Nov 18) a 31.3 per cent year-on-year increase in earnings to S$13 million for its third quarter ended Sep 30. Revenue grew 12.8 per cent to S$238.5 million, from S$211.5 million a year earlier. The increase was mainly driven by Frencken’s mechatronics division’s revenue, which rose 13.4 per cent to S$214.3 million. The counter ended S$0.01, or 0.6 per cent, up at S$1.71 before the news.

data.title: When AI systems are compromised, detection without recovery is not resilience
data.description:
RECENT data breaches involving MoneySmart, M1 and Doctor Anywhere have put cyber risks back in focus for Singapore businesses.

On Nov 13, the Cyber Security Agency of Singapore urged all organisations to “take immediate steps to strengthen their cyberdefences”.

While most conversations have focused on how these incidents happened and what information was exposed, they raise a bigger, more urgent question for business leaders. If critical systems are hit, how long can the business afford to be out of action before the financial, operational and reputational damage begin to pile up?

Consider two incidents with very different outcomes.

In September 2026, Boustead Singapore disclosed that an overseas business unit had isolated affected systems, activated business continuity procedures and recovered critical data and systems from backups following a cyberincident. Its operations suffered no material disruption.

Contrast that with the 2025 cyberattack on Marks & Spencer, which forced systems offline and disrupted online operations for weeks. While physical stores continued trading, customers could not access certain online shopping services, with operations returning in phases.

The circumstances were different, but both incidents highlight a key point. Getting systems back online is one thing; knowing whether the business can safely resume operations is another.

As organisations give artificial-intelligence agents access to sensitive systems, leaders must ask: Can the team determine what happened, contain the consequences and safely reverse unintended outcomes?

Commvault’s 2026 State of Data Resilience report found that only 45 per cent of organisations in Singapore are very confident that they could identify a compromised AI system.

If organisations are not even confident they can identify a compromised AI system, determining what has been affected, what needs to be recovered, and whether the team can restore it to a clean, trusted state could be even more challenging.

AI changes the nature of the blast radius

As AI moves from assisting employees to acting on their behalf, the nature of operational risk changes.

An autonomous AI agent may make decisions and take actions across multiple connected systems using identities and permissions legitimately granted by the organisation.

This autonomy creates business value, but it also means that a compromised identity, inaccurate data, incomplete instruction or poorly designed workflow can trigger consequences across data, applications and business processes before a person has time to intervene.

The challenge then is to understand the chain of actions that followed.

What data did the system access? What decisions did it influence? Which transactions did it initiate? What downstream processes accepted its output? Which actions need to be reversed, reconciled or reviewed?

Without that understanding, an organisation cannot know whether the incident is truly contained.

And if it cannot establish which data and systems remain trustworthy, restoring the affected technology may not be enough.

Recover what the business needs, then prove that it works

No organisation can restore everything at once. Recovery, therefore, needs to begin with understanding which capabilities the business needs first, and what those capabilities depend on.

The minimum viable company, or MVC, defines the systems, data and operations that must remain available, or be restored first, for the organisation to continue functioning during disruption.

An MVC differs by organisation.

For a bank, it might include enabling customers to make time-critical payments and withdraw funds. For a logistics provider, it might mean accepting shipping instructions, tracking goods in transit and releasing deliveries at their destination.

The priority is to determine which business processes must continue or be restored first, and then map the systems, data, people and other dependencies needed to support them.

The same principle applies to AI. One business process supported by AI may require rapid recovery, while another one may tolerate a longer interruption.

Prioritisation should therefore be based on business impact and recovery requirements, not simply on whether a workload uses AI.

It must also account for the identities, applications, infrastructure and data required to restore the complete business process safely.

Boards do not need to know every recovery dependency or direct the operational response.

But they should require evidence that management has identified the organisation’s critical business capabilities, and agreed on the order in which they will be restored cleanly and tested so that they can operate safely following disruption.

The next test for trusted AI: Recovery readiness

As Singapore advances trusted AI, resilience must become part of that trust. Guardrails matter, but so does knowing the business can recover when those are not enough.

As AI moves from assisting to acting, recovery readiness must become part of AI readiness.

Singapore businesses must be able to demonstrate that they can contain unintended consequences, restore critical operations and recover safely when existing safeguards fall short.
